lead: Light and matter are not purely waves or purely particles. Light carries energy in packets called photons, yet it bends and interferes like a wave. An electron can diffract like a wave, yet it lands as one dot on a detector. This chapter builds that picture from black-body radiation, Planck's quantum, the photoelectric effect, de Broglie waves and electron diffraction. It then states Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, which limits how sharply position and momentum can be fixed together. These ideas explain atomic spectra, electron microscopes and why electrons in atoms do not fall into the nucleus. Only a few universities teach this in first semester.
prereq: You need school physics: waves, photons and kinetic energy; the next step, putting matter waves into an equation, is in 1.2.

sections.h3: Black-body radiation, quanta and the photoelectric effect

blocks.text: A black body absorbs and emits all wavelengths. Its spectrum is continuous; as temperature T rises, the peak moves to shorter wavelength. Classical wave theory failed at short wavelength. In 1900 Planck proposed that atoms emit or absorb energy only in packets called quanta. One quantum has energy E = hν, where h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is Planck's constant and ν is frequency in s⁻¹. An oscillator has E = nhν, with n = 0, 1, 2, ...

Light of frequency ν falls on a metal and ejects electrons. Emission starts only above a threshold ν₀, and it is immediate. The fastest electron has KE_max = hν − φ, where φ is the work function in J. Brighter light gives more electrons, not faster ones. Wave theory predicts energy from intensity, so it fails. Light therefore arrives as photons, each with energy hν and momentum p = h/λ, where λ is wavelength in m. Interference and diffraction show the wave face of light.

sections.h3: Matter waves and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle

blocks.text: Louis de Broglie proposed that matter has wavelength λ = h/p = h/(mv). Here p is momentum in kg m s⁻¹, m is mass in kg and v is speed in m s⁻¹. For a moving electron this wavelength is of atomic size. A beam of electrons passed through a thin crystal forms diffraction rings. The measured ring spacing agrees with λ = h/p. Large objects have tiny λ, so their waves are not seen.

Heisenberg's uncertainty principle says position x and momentum p cannot both be sharp. For repeated measurements, Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2. Here Δx is the standard deviation of position in m, Δp is the standard deviation of momentum in kg m s⁻¹, and ħ = h/(2π) = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. The limit is not caused by clumsy instruments. An electron confined to Δx ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m has Δp ≥ ħ/(2Δx) ≈ 5 × 10⁻²⁵ kg m s⁻¹, comparable with atomic momenta. So an electron cannot sit still at a point. This is why atoms have minimum energy; 1.2 turns the idea into an equation.

figure.caption: The curve is the minimum Δp = 0.5/Δx in scaled units; points above it are allowed by Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2. Notice that a tighter position (small Δx) forces a larger momentum spread.

spec.aria: A hyperbola shows the smallest allowed momentum spread falling as position spread grows; points above the curve are allowed.

examples.question: A photon has wavelength 400 nm. Its momentum is known to 0.1%. Find its momentum and the minimum position uncertainty. Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and ħ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
examples.answer: p = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m s⁻¹; minimum Δx = 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ m = 0.032 mm.

lam = 400e-9
p = h / lam
dp = 0.001 * p
hbar = 1.055e-34
dx = hbar / (2 * dp)
print(f"{p:.3g}")
print(f"{dp:.3g}")
print(f"{dx:.2g}")

traps: Δx is the standard deviation of many position measurements, not the particle's diameter.
Photon momentum is h/λ; a photon has zero rest mass, so p = mc does not apply.
Electron diffraction shows matter waves; the photoelectric effect shows light particles.

quiz.q: Write E = hν and define the symbols.
quiz.a: E is quantum energy in J; h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; ν is frequency in s⁻¹.

quiz.q: Why does photoelectric emission depend on frequency, not intensity?
quiz.a: Each photon carries hν; only ν ≥ ν₀ gives enough energy to escape. Intensity changes photon number, not photon energy.

quiz.q: An electron has λ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Find p.
If Δx doubles, what happens to the minimum Δp?

beyond: Not for the exam. The same ideas set the scale of quantum dots, electron microscopes and tunnelling diodes. Scanning tunnelling microscopes use the tail of an electron wave to image atoms. Quantum computing uses controlled superposition, not classical bits. Search next for electron diffraction, tunnelling and the Heisenberg microscope.
